Three-Body Observatory

One equation governs every system of three stars, planets or moons. There is no formula that solves it, so this page solves it the way astronomers do: numerically, live in your browser, to about twelve significant digits.

The equation

Every body pulls on every other body

Give each body a position and a mass . Newton's law of gravitation and his second law combine into one equation per body:

G is the gravitational constant. ε is an optional softening length; real point masses have ε = 0, which is the default here.

That line is fully general. Stars, planets, moons and black holes (far from the horizon) all obey it. The only inputs are three masses and the starting positions and velocities. Written out for three bodies it is:

That makes 18 coupled first-order differential equations: three position components and three velocity components for each body. The same system in Hamiltonian form, which is what the solver actually works with:

The triangle form

Lagrange noticed you can drop the centre of mass entirely and follow the triangle's sides instead. With , the sides always close up, and each obeys a Kepler law plus one shared coupling term:

Without the coupling term S each side would be an independent two-body problem with a closed-form ellipse. That one shared term is where all the difficulty lives.

Planets or stars: one equation at any scale

Pick a length unit L and a mass unit M. Measuring time in units of t* removes G from the equation completely:

So one dimensionless solution describes every system with the same mass ratios and shape. The simulator runs with G = 1. This converter turns its time units into real ones:

t* = 58.13 days
Conservation

Ten numbers never change

Energy (one number), momentum (three), angular momentum (three) and the steady drift of the centre of mass (three) are fixed by the starting conditions. They shrink the 18-dimensional space of possible states to 8 dimensions.

For two bodies that is enough to solve the motion exactly: Kepler's ellipses. For three it is not, and it never will be. Bruns (1887) proved there are no other conserved quantities that are algebraic in positions and velocities. Poincaré (1890) proved there are no further analytic ones. The motion is not confined to any simpler surface that a formula could describe.

The instrument rail above tracks two of these live. At the default tolerance (10⁻¹²) the energy of Burrau's problem stays within a few parts in 10¹¹ of its starting value and ends there after the ejection. During the tightest encounters the reading can jump to 10⁻⁸ for a step or two. At a close pericentre the kinetic and potential energies are both enormous, so their difference is only known to about U × tolerance; the reading settles back once the pair separates. If the error stays above 10⁻⁶, the status line says so.

Solving it

What "solving the three-body problem" can mean

There is no general closed-form solution. That is a theorem, not a gap in current knowledge. Three kinds of answer exist instead.

1. A series that converges and is useless

Karl Sundman (1912) proved that the positions can be written as power series that converge for all time whenever the angular momentum is not zero. He did it by regularizing collisions and mapping all of time into a disk:

It is a true solution in the mathematical sense. In practice the series converges so slowly that Beloriszky (1930) estimated about 108,000,000 terms would be needed for ordinary astronomical accuracy.

2. Exact special solutions

Euler (1767) and Lagrange (1772) found families where the bodies keep the same shape forever. Both work for any three masses, and the simulator rebuilds them for whatever masses you set. Lagrange's equilateral triangle rotates at

It is stable only when one mass dominates, by Routh's criterion (1875):

Equal masses fail it, so the equal-mass triangle eventually breaks apart. Rounding errors of 10⁻¹⁶ grow exponentially until they matter. Euler's collinear solution places the bodies on a rotating line, with spacing ratio λ fixed by the single positive root of Euler's quintic:

Since 2013 computer searches have found thousands of further periodic orbits; the butterflies, moths and yin-yangs in the System menu (Šuvakov & Dmitrašinović 2013) are among them. The figure-eight is older: Moore found it numerically in 1993 and Chenciner and Montgomery proved it exists in 2000. Every periodic orbit in the menu, the figure-eight included, was refined here with Newton's method, which tightens the published starting values from about 10⁻³ closure to about 10⁻¹².

3. Numerical integration with controlled error

This is how the problem is solved in practice, and what this page does. For any starting conditions and any finite span of time, the solver produces the motion to a chosen accuracy. The limit is chaos. A tiny difference δ₀ grows exponentially:

Double-precision numbers start at δ₀ ≈ 10⁻¹⁶. A system with Lyapunov exponent λ = 1 therefore loses all predictability after roughly 35 time units, no matter how good the solver is. Switch on the Butterfly twin in the simulator: it runs a second copy displaced by δ and measures λ for whatever system you load.

The solver

Regularized Bulirsch–Stoer

The equations blow up when two bodies meet: the 1/r³ term goes to infinity. An ordinary solver takes smaller and smaller steps there and either stalls or fails. This page integrates in a fictitious time s instead, chosen so that close encounters are stretched out:

A leapfrog split of these equations keeps any two-body orbit exactly on its Kepler ellipse, even straight through a collision (Mikkola & Tanikawa 1999; Preto & Tremaine 1999). Bulirsch–Stoer extrapolation then runs the leapfrog with 2, 4, 6, … substeps and extrapolates to zero step size. That gives roughly tenth-order accuracy plus an error estimate, which sets the step size automatically.

Two details matter for getting the right answer. First, the solver integrates the three sides of the triangle from the triangle form above, not absolute positions. Positions near x = 0.5 carry about 16 digits, so a pair 10⁻⁹ apart would have its separation known to only 7; each side as its own variable keeps a tight pair at full precision wherever it is. Second, every operation on the integration path is one that IEEE-754 requires to be correctly rounded (+ − × ÷ √), so every browser engine takes bit-identical steps. That is what lets a fate-map pixel computed offline replay exactly here.

The same algorithm runs here in JavaScript and in the repository's Python package. Everything below is checked by its test suite, at tolerance 10⁻¹²:

  • Burrau's Pythagorean problem (masses 3, 4, 5 released from rest) ends with mass 3 ejected at t ≈ 60 and masses 4 and 5 in a binary with eccentricity 0.99, as Szebehely and Peters found in 1967. Energy is conserved to 3 × 10⁻¹¹ at t = 80, after a closest approach of 0.0004.
  • Agrees with SciPy's 8th-order DOP853 integrator to 2 × 10⁻¹⁰ after 15 time units of chaotic motion.
  • From its 8-digit published starting values the figure-eight closes to 3 × 10⁻⁸ after one period, the limit of those digits. From the refined values it closes to 7 × 10⁻¹³.
  • Lagrange triangles stay equilateral to 3 × 10⁻¹³, and Euler lines stay collinear, for unequal masses.
  • A head-on collision passes through in 39 steps with energy error 6 × 10⁻¹⁰, and gives the same result when the whole system is shifted away from the origin.

Fate map

Who gets thrown out, and when?

Release three equal masses from rest. Bodies 1 and 2 start at (−½, 0) and (½, 0); body 3 starts at the point you pick. Almost every such system ends the same way: two bodies pair up and the third is flung away. Which one goes, and when, depends on the starting point in a way no formula can capture.

Each of the 96,000 pixels below is a full integration with the same solver, run until a body escapes or t = 200. Brightness shows how soon a body escapes; switch the view to see which one. Click any pixel to run that system in the simulator. It will play out exactly as computed here.

The map holds a built-in experiment. Its left and right halves are mirror images, so in exact arithmetic they would match pixel for pixel. Both halves were integrated independently, and their floating-point rounding differs in the 16th digit. In the smooth bands, where neighbouring starts share a fate, the halves agree on the escaping body for 99.9% of pixels. In the speckled regions they agree on only 71%. There, a difference of one part in 1016 decides which star is thrown out.

Pixels in plum (157 of them, 0.16%) are marked unresolved: their run hit the step limit, or ended with an energy error above 10⁻⁶. They are left uncoloured rather than guessed.
